introduction: IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) nomenclature is the standard system for naming chemical compounds. The rules below summarise how to name inorganic and organic compounds systematically.

binaryCompounds.name: Inorganic Binary Compounds
rules: The element farther left in the periodic table is named first (e.g., sodium chloride).
The element farther right is named second with the suffix -ide (e.g., chloride, oxide).
Greek prefixes (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-, hepta-, octa-, nona-, deca-) are used for covalent (non-metal) compounds to indicate the count of each atom.
The prefix 'mono-' is usually omitted for the first element.
Roman numerals in parentheses indicate the oxidation state of the metal in ionic compounds (Stock system).

ionicCompounds.name: Ionic Compounds
ionicCompounds.description: Compounds formed between a metal and a nonmetal (or polyatomic ion).
rules: Cation (positive) is named first using the element name; anion (negative) follows with the -ide suffix.
For polyatomic ions, use the standard ion name (e.g., sulfate, nitrate, carbonate).
If the metal can have multiple oxidation states, use Roman numerals (Stock system) or the -ous/-ic suffix.
Crossover rule (Crisscross method) is used to balance charges when writing the formula.
Ammonium salts use the name 'ammonium' for the cation.
Named as 'hydro-<root>-ic acid'. Example: HCl is hydrochloric acid.
Use the stem of the element (chlor-, brom-, fluor-, sulfur-) plus -ic.
If the polyatomic ion ends in -ate, the acid ends in -ic acid. Example: SO4^2- → H2SO4 is sulfuric acid.
If the polyatomic ion ends in -ite, the acid ends in -ous acid. Example: SO3^2- → H2SO3 is sulfurous acid.
If the polyatomic ion ends in -ide, use hydro-...-ic acid (binary acid).
Per- prefix means one more oxygen (e.g., ClO4- is perchlorate → HClO4 is perchloric acid).
Hypo- prefix means one less oxygen (e.g., ClO- is hypochlorite → HClO is hypochlorous acid).

alkanes.name: Alkanes
rules: Use Greek prefix for carbon count (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-, non-, dec-) plus -ane.
For branched alkanes, identify the longest chain, then add substituents as prefixes.

alkenes.name: Alkenes
alkenes.description: Hydrocarbons with at least one C=C double bond; formula CnH2n.
rules: Same as alkanes but the suffix is -ene.
The position of the double bond is given by the lower-numbered carbon (e.g., but-2-ene).
For multiple double bonds, use -adiene, -atriene, etc.

alkynes.name: Alkynes
alkynes.description: Hydrocarbons with at least one C≡C triple bond; formula CnH2n-2.
rules: Same as alkanes but the suffix is -yne.
Number the chain to give the triple bond the lowest locant.

substitutedAlkane.name: Naming a Substituted Alkane
substitutedAlkane.description: Step-by-step procedure for naming complex organic molecules.

steps.name: Find the longest carbon chain
steps.detail: The longest chain becomes the parent name (methane, ethane, propane, etc.).

steps.name: Number the chain to give the lowest locants
steps.detail: Number from the end that gives the substituent (or the first point of unsaturation) the lowest number.

steps.name: Identify and name substituents
steps.detail: Each group off the main chain is named (methyl, ethyl, chloro, bromo, hydroxy, etc.). Use locants to indicate their position.

steps.name: Alphabetize substituents
steps.detail: List substituents in alphabetical order. Ignore the di-, tri-, etc. prefixes for alphabetising, but include them when naming.

steps.name: Assemble the name
steps.detail: Combine: locant(s)-substituent(s) + parent name + locant-suffix. For example: 2,3-dimethylbutane.

example.solution: Identify the longest chain (4 carbons) → butane; find the methyl substituent at carbon 2; final name: 2-methylbutane

functionalGroups.name: Functional Group Priority for Suffix
functionalGroups.description: When a molecule has multiple functional groups, the highest-priority group becomes the suffix; others are named as prefixes.

stereochemistry.name: Stereochemistry Prefixes
stereochemistry.description: Descriptors used to indicate three-dimensional configuration.

prefixes.use: Two same groups on same side of a double bond or ring
Two same groups on opposite sides of a double bond or ring
Rectus (clockwise) absolute configuration at a stereocentre (CIP priority rules)
Sinister (counter-clockwise) absolute configuration at a stereocentre
Entgegen (opposite side) — high-priority groups on opposite sides of a double bond
Zusammen (together) — high-priority groups on the same side of a double bond
Dextrorotatory in Fischer projection of sugars/amino acids

summary: Use Greek prefixes for non-metal binary compounds.
Use Roman numerals (Stock system) for metals with variable oxidation state.
Oxyacids are named after their parent polyatomic ion (-ic acid for -ate; -ous acid for -ite).
When multiple functional groups are present, only the highest-priority group is named as a suffix; others become prefixes.
Stereochemistry uses cis/trans or E/Z (for double bonds) and R/S (for stereocentres).
